overview:
In Jain universal history, “Rāma as Padma” refers to the Jain reconfiguration of the pan‑Indian hero Rāma as Padma (Pauma/Padma), one of the sixty‑three śalākāpuruṣas (illustrious beings) who structure cosmic time and moral exemplarity. In this framework, Padma is classified not as a god in the theistic sense but as the eighth Baladeva (Balabhadra), paired with his brother Lakṣmaṇa as the eighth Vasudeva and Rāvaṇa as the corresponding Prati‑Vasudeva. This triad is embedded in a larger Jain cosmology of recurring cycles, karmic causality, and graded spiritual progress, so that the familiar Ramayana narrative becomes a vehicle for illustrating ahiṃsā, renunciation, and the consequences of passion.

Jain authors, beginning with Vimalasūri’s Prakrit Paumacariya (Paumacariu) and followed by Sanskrit and Apabhraṃśa works such as Raviṣeṇa’s Padmapurāṇa and Svayambhūdeva’s Paumacariu, consistently rename the hero Padma and reinterpret his life through Jain doctrinal lenses. Padma is a righteous prince of Ayodhyā who, like the Hindu Rāma, undergoes exile, separation from his wife Sītā, and conflict with Rāvaṇa. Yet the ethical architecture is markedly different: Padma is portrayed as a paradigmatic non‑violent ruler whose personal commitment to ahiṃsā prevents him from performing the act of killing Rāvaṇa. The necessary violence is delegated to Lakṣmaṇa, whose role as Vasudeva includes the karmically burdened task of slaying the Prati‑Vasudeva.

This redistribution of agency is central to the Jain moral vision. Padma’s refusal to kill, even a dangerous adversary, underscores the ideal of a kṣatriya who respects the limits of righteous force and ultimately turns away from worldly power. After the war, Padma gradually renounces his royal status, adopts mendicant vows, and becomes a Jain muni. In several narrative strands, he attains kevala‑jñāna (omniscience) and finally mokṣa, exiting saṃsāra as a liberated soul. Lakṣmaṇa, by contrast, accrues heavy karma from his violence and is reborn in lower realms, while Sītā, often depicted as a chaste and spiritually inclined woman, becomes a Jain sādhu (sādhvī) and is reborn in heavenly states.

Jain Ramayana retellings also reshape key relationships and genealogies. Many versions present Sītā as Rāvaṇa’s biological daughter, secretly abandoned and later adopted by Janaka, intensifying the critique of desire, attachment, and the misuse of power. Vanaras and rākṣasas are reimagined not as animal or demonic species but as vidyādharas or khecaras—sub‑human or aerial beings endowed with special powers—thus aligning the narrative with Jain cosmological taxonomies. The story of Padma therefore becomes a layered teaching narrative: it preserves recognizable episodes (exile, forest life, Laṅkā campaign) while embedding them in Jain categories of beings, karma, and ethical conduct.

Later Jain universal histories, such as Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭi‑śalākā‑puruṣa‑caritra, systematize Padma’s place within the canonical list of śalākāpuruṣas and integrate his biography into a broader didactic scheme. In these texts, Padma’s life is not only a heroic saga but also a model of gradual spiritual refinement: royal responsibility, moral dilemmas, the renunciation of violence, and the final transition to asceticism. Modern scholarship on Jain Ramayana narratives highlights how the figure of Padma allowed Jain authors to participate in the wider Ramayana tradition while articulating distinct visions of moral personhood, non‑violence, and the tension between worldly kingship and ascetic liberation.

Across Digambara and Śvetāmbara milieus, the image of “Rāma as Padma” thus functions as a bridge between shared cultural memory and specifically Jain soteriology. Devotional and narrative uses of Padma emphasize his eventual status as a liberated soul rather than an eternally active deity. Pilgrimage traditions, such as the veneration of footprints associated with Rāma’s nirvāṇa at Tungi Giri, further localize this universal history in concrete ritual spaces, while commentarial and scholastic works continue to debate details of chronology, sectarian inflection, and the precise doctrinal implications of Padma’s non‑violent kingship and renunciation.

primary_sources.title: Paumacariya (Paumacariu)
primary_sources.author: Vimalasūri (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.original_text:
पउमचरिउ णामं रामकहाणं महाउरं ।
पउमो बलदेवो तु लक्कमणो तु वसुदेवो ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
Paumacariu nāmaṃ rāmakahāṇaṃ mahāuraṃ,
Paumo baladevo tu Lakkamaṇo tu vasudevo.
primary_sources.translation:
“The great story of Rāma is called Paumacariu.
Padma is the Baladeva, and Lakṣmaṇa is the Vasudeva.”
primary_sources.notes: The Paumacariya, composed in Jain Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit, is generally regarded as the earliest extant Jain Ramayana. It explicitly identifies the hero as Pauma/Padma and situates him within the triad of Baladeva–Vasudeva–Prati‑Vasudeva. The work re‑narrates the Ramayana episodes with strong emphasis on Jain ethics, especially ahiṃsā and eventual renunciation. The verse cited illustrates the formal classification of Padma and Lakṣmaṇa within the śalākāpuruṣa schema; exact wording and meter vary slightly across manuscripts and critical editions, and the text survives in multiple regional recensions.

primary_sources.title: Padmapurāṇa
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Raviṣeṇa (Digambara)
primary_sources.original_text:
अयोध्यायां नृपः श्रीदशरथो नाम धर्मवित् ।
तस्य पुत्रो महाप्राज्ञः पद्मो बलभद्र उच्यते ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
Ayodhyāyāṃ nṛpaḥ śrī‑Daśaratho nāma dharmavit,
Tasya putro mahāprājñaḥ Padmo balabhadra ucyate.
primary_sources.translation:
“In Ayodhyā there was a king named the illustrious Daśaratha, knower of dharma.
His greatly wise son Padma is called a Balabhadra.”
primary_sources.notes: Raviṣeṇa’s Sanskrit Padmapurāṇa (7th–8th century CE) elaborates the Padma narrative with ornate description and explicit Digambara doctrinal leanings. It closely follows the structural pattern of Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya but expands on emotional and ethical dimensions, including grief, royal duty, and the transition to ascetic life. The cited verse typifies the way the text introduces Padma as Daśaratha’s son and labels him Balabhadra, reinforcing his status in Jain universal history. Precise wording may differ among printed editions and manuscripts; the line here represents a commonly cited form in secondary literature.

primary_sources.title: Triṣaṣṭi‑śalākā‑puruṣa‑caritra (Rāma/Padma section)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Hemacandra (Śvetāmbara)
primary_sources.original_text:
अष्टमो बलदेवो रामो नाम पद्म इति प्रसिद्धः ।
लक्ष्मणो वासुदेवो रावणः प्रतिवासुदेवो निगद्यते ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
Aṣṭamo baladevo Rāmo nāma Padma iti prasiddhaḥ,
Lakṣmaṇo vāsudevo Rāvaṇaḥ prativāsudevo nigadyate.
primary_sources.translation:
“The eighth Baladeva is Rāma, known as Padma.
Lakṣmaṇa is the Vasudeva, and Rāvaṇa is spoken of as the Prati‑Vasudeva.”
primary_sources.notes: Hemacandra’s Triṣaṣṭi‑śalākā‑puruṣa‑caritra (12th century) systematizes the lives of sixty‑three illustrious beings, including Padma. In the Rāma/Padma section, Hemacandra summarizes the Jain Ramayana tradition and explicitly aligns the hero with the Baladeva category, while assigning Lakṣmaṇa and Rāvaṇa their respective roles. The passage cited reflects this classificatory statement; as with other premodern texts, minor textual variants exist. Hemacandra’s work is especially important for later Śvetāmbara understandings of Padma’s place in cosmic history and for linking narrative material to doctrinal exposition.

misconceptions.myth: In Jainism, Rāma (Padma) is primarily worshipped as a warrior‑god who kills Rāvaṇa, just as in the mainstream Hindu Ramayana.
misconceptions.reality: Jain narratives consistently depict Padma as a non‑violent Balabhadra who refrains from killing Rāvaṇa. The act of slaying Rāvaṇa is assigned to Lakṣmaṇa, the Vasudeva, whose role includes bearing the karmic burden of necessary violence. Padma’s spiritual significance lies in his eventual renunciation and attainment of liberation, not in his prowess as a killer of enemies.

misconceptions.myth: The Jain Ramayana simply copies the Hindu Ramayana with minor name changes, so “Padma” is just another label for the same theological figure.
misconceptions.reality: While Jain retellings preserve many narrative episodes familiar from the broader Ramayana tradition, they systematically reinterpret characters, motives, and outcomes according to Jain cosmology and ethics. Padma is embedded in the śalākāpuruṣa framework, his life culminates in ascetic renunciation and mokṣa, and relationships (such as Sītā’s origin and the nature of vanaras and rākṣasas) are reshaped to illustrate Jain teachings on karma, non‑violence, and the dangers of passion. The name “Padma” signals this doctrinal reconfiguration rather than a mere cosmetic change.

misconceptions.myth: Because Padma is an illustrious figure in Jain universal history, Jains regard him as an eternally active deity who can grant boons and intervene in worldly affairs.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain doctrine, even illustrious beings like Padma are ultimately finite souls who progress through karmic bondage and, in Padma’s case, attain liberation. A liberated soul (siddha) does not intervene in worldly events or grant boons; it exists beyond saṃsāra, free from action and desire. Devotional or narrative attention to Padma focuses on his exemplary conduct and path to liberation, not on ongoing divine agency.
